sources: Johns Hopkins Medicine news release via ScienceDaily, 'Owl mystery unraveled' (Jan 31, 2013; F. de Kok-Mercado, P. Gailloud): owls turn their heads as much as 270 degrees in either direction; study of snowy, barred and great horned owls; bony holes around the vertebral artery about 10 times larger than the artery; 12 of the 14 cervical vertebrae; contractile blood reservoirs at the base of the head pool blood for their large brains and eyes; in humans sudden neck twists can tear artery linings and cause stroke; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/01/130131144102.htm

Smithsonian Magazine, 'Solving the Mystery of Owls' Head-Turning Abilities' (2013): up to 270 degrees in either direction; adaptation found in 12 of 14 neck vertebrae; dye pooled in reservoirs near the base of the skull; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/solving-the-mystery-of-owls-head-turning-abilities-9561557/

National Geographic, 'How Owls Twist Their Heads Almost 360 Degrees': maximum 270 degrees; owls have fixed eye sockets so their eyeballs can't rotate; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/how-owls-twist-heads-almost-360-degrees

Audubon Magazine, 'The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained': comb-like serrations on the leading edge of wing feathers break up turbulent air; a velvety texture and a soft trailing-edge fringe dampen sound; owls can fly virtually silently; large owls such as the Barn Owl can fly as slowly as two mph; study of 70 owl species (K. Le Piane); https://www.audubon.org/magazine/silent-flight-of-owls-explained

University of Illinois College of Veterinary Medicine, Owl Pellet worksheet (Wildlife Encounters): owls have no crop and no teeth; food is swallowed whole; about 12 hours after eating the owl regurgitates undigested material as a pellet; https://vetmed.illinois.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/OwlPelletWorksheet_WildlifeEncounters.pdf

beats.say: An owl can turn its head two hundred seventy degrees. Without choking off its own brain.
The owl. And no, it can't go all the way around. That's a myth.
Its eyeballs are locked in place. They can't roll around like yours.
So it turns its whole head instead, on fourteen neck bones.
Twist your neck that hard, and you could tear an artery, and have a stroke.
So how does the owl survive it?
Scientists at Johns Hopkins injected dye into dead owls' necks to find out.
The holes in its neck bones are ten times wider than the artery inside.
So the artery has room to twist, without getting pinched.
And at the base of its head, blood pools in little reserve tanks,
to keep its big brain and big eyes fed while the head turns.
Then it takes off. And you hear almost nothing.
Its wing feathers have a comb along the front edge that breaks up the air.
A barn owl can fly as slow as two miles an hour.
Now the gross part. An owl has no teeth. It swallows small prey whole.
About twelve hours later, it coughs up a pellet of bones and fur.
Would you pick up an owl pellet?
It eats dinner whole, and hands you back the skeleton.
